Hormuz: The Tollbooth Adds a Cleanup Fee

Iran says no ship can cross the Strait of Hormuz safely without Tehran’s approval and supervision. Washington calls that fiction. 

Tehran calls Washington’s intelligence fake. The shipping industry calls it a route where normal traffic has become a rumor.

Iran’s goal is no longer subtle: turn wartime control into a permanent maritime franchise. 

Tehran has sought an arrangement that would let it vet ships, route traffic through lanes hugging Iranian waters, and eventually charge for passage. 

Reuters reported that some vessels outside government-to-government arrangements have paid Iranian authorities more than $150,000 for purported security and navigation services.

The problem with building a maritime order through coercion is that customers begin asking whether the security service caused the insecurity.

Traffic is still nowhere near normal. Before the war, roughly 125 to 140 vessels transited the strait each day; during the crisis, the count fell to only a handful daily, according to ship-tracking data cited by Reuters. 

The reported U.S. position is blunt: any temporary arrangement must exclude tolls or transit fees.

Then came the oil slick near Qeshm Island.

Iranian officials initially tied the pollution to attacks on tankers in the strait. The source has not been independently established, but reports describe repeated strikes on tankers and mounting environmental damage along Iranian shores.

Tehran’s revised logic is almost elegant: any party that profits from transit through Hormuz should repair the environmental damage it causes.

So the power claiming the right to inspect the route may also claim the right to invoice it — for passage, “services,” security and the mess left behind.

Meanwhile, Iranian sources say the UAE released additional frozen Iranian assets, including at least 1.5 tons of gold allegedly worth about $212 million.

 The claim is unverified, and Abu Dhabi previously denied reports that it had agreed to unlock up to $20 billion in Iranian funds, describing them as “completely false and unfounded.”

The gold story may be true, false or useful before it is true.

But the political message needs no assay: Tehran wants more than a strait. It wants a customs desk, an insurance office and an environmental claims department — all operating under the same flag.

📣 Brazil stablecoins face IMF scrutiny as crypto flows outpace capital 

🌐 IMF has called for closer oversight of Brazil’s stablecoin market as cross-border crypto flows outpace traditional capital movements. The report says cross-border crypto transactions have increased faster than conventional capital flows and now require closer regulatory attention because of their growing links with the country’s financial system. The assessment says stablecoin purchases respond much more strongly to global financial shocks than traditional portfolio investment or foreign direct investment. 

🔔 Based on the IMF’s analysis, purchases of dollar-backed stablecoins are two to three times more sensitive to external market events, raising concerns over how quickly international volatility could spread through crypto markets. Brazil has emerged as one of the world’s more active crypto markets, with stablecoins accounting for a significant share of digital asset activity. The IMF said the country’s crypto ecosystem has become increasingly connected with the traditional financial sector, making regulatory oversight more important as adoption continues to rise.

⚠️ The report acknowledges that Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) has already introduced measures to regulate crypto asset service providers. Even so, the IMF said several areas still need stronger rules, including customer asset protection, stablecoin issuance requirements, and compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) standards.

🇺🇸🏁 Bloomberg: US sends NATO allies loyalty questionnaire ahead of troop cuts

Washington has circulated a document to NATO members gauging their support for Trump's foreign policy before deciding on further cuts to US military assets in Europe.

The questionnaire asks whether each country has "been publicly supportive" of US foreign policy, what restrictions it has placed on American forces using its bases, and whether it's "willing to reduce or eliminate" those restrictions.

It also probes defense spending: whether allies are buying US defense products, meeting budget commitments, and whether they've publicly opposed "Made in Europe" procurement initiatives that favor local firms over American ones.

One question asks bluntly whether the country's conduct matches Washington's preferred posture: firm alignment with the US, without public criticism.

Sources say the document touches on several flashpoints dividing Washington from NATO, including the US strikes on Iran and the operation to kidnap Maduro in Venezuela, both carried out without allied consultation.

Allies reportedly reacted negatively, calling it an attempt to force ideological alignment in exchange for US protection.

The questionnaire first circulated in Washington before reaching NATO HQ in Brussels. The US will meet allies there later this month to discuss the ongoing review, which is expected to result in further American troop reductions in Europe.
